stages.title: Advanced vocabulary and terminology
explain: Advanced vocabulary depends on word formation. Prefixes and suffixes build families: "possible, impossible, possibilité, impossibilité". Suffixes mark categories: -ment (adverb), -tion (action noun), -eur (agent), -able (capable of). Register shifts the vocabulary: "commencer" (standard) and "débuter" or "entamer" (more formal).

Near-synonyms differ in collocation. One "prend une décision", "fait une erreur" and "pose une question". Specialist terms often come from Latin and Greek, which is why French shares many roots with English, but beware of nuance: "éventuellement" means possibly, not eventually (which is "finalement").
sentences: We must take a decision soon.
The stakes are high for everyone.

gq.why: It is a false friend of eventually.

gq.q: Why do learners say "faire une décision" wrongly?
o: The collocation in French is prendre une décision
gq.why: Collocations are not predictable from English.

panel.q: Which suffix typically forms an action noun?
panel.why: -tion names an action or its result, as in organisation.

panel.q: Which verb is the most formal for "to begin"?
panel.why: Entamer and débuter belong to a higher register than commencer.

panel.q: Why does knowing word roots help reading a technical text?
o: Roots reveal meaning even in unfamiliar words
It makes reading faster in speech only
panel.why: Many technical terms share Latin and Greek roots.

teach.model: Advanced vocabulary is built from roots, prefixes and suffixes. Learn collocations like prendre une décision. Check register and watch false friends such as éventuellement.

stages.hook: Why can the word "plutôt" mean "rather" in one sentence and "instead" in another, and how do advanced learners handle such nuance?
stages.mnemonic: Build the word from its roots, then check its company.

stages.title: Academic language
explain: Academic French values an impersonal, precise and structured style. Writers use the passive voice, impersonal structures ("il convient de", "il s'agit de") and nominalisation: "L'augmentation des prix a entraîné une baisse de la demande." The author often says "nous" even when alone (the "nous de modestie").

Typical structure is problématique (the research question), plan (outline) and argumentation. Connectors build logic: "en effet", "certes... mais", "dès lors", "par ailleurs", "autrement dit". Academic citation means giving the author, work and year, and quoting precisely with guillemets « ».
sentences: In other words, the hypothesis is false.
It is a matter of method.
The rise in prices reduced demand.

gq.why: Autrement dit means in other words.

gq.q: Why use the impersonal "il convient de" in academic writing?

panel.q: What does "nominalisation" do in a sentence?
o: Turns a verb into a noun to condense ideas
Turns a noun into a verb
panel.why: It increases density and abstraction.

panel.q: Which punctuation marks quotations in French?
panel.why: Guillemets are the standard French quotation marks.

panel.q: Why does a dissertation begin with a problématique?
o: It defines the question the whole argument answers
panel.why: A clear question guides the structure.

teach.model: Academic French is impersonal and structured. It uses passive and impersonal phrases like il convient de, nominalisation and logical connectors. A text starts with a problématique, follows a plan and ends with a conclusion. Quotations use guillemets.

stages.hook: Why do academic French texts often avoid "je" and use "on" or "nous" instead?
stages.mnemonic: Question, plan, proof, conclusion: the French dissertation spine.

stages.title: Professional communication
explain: Professional French is formal, polite and indirect. Emails open with "Madame, Monsieur," or "Bonjour Madame Durand," and close with "Cordialement" or "Bien cordialement". Typical phrases: "Veuillez trouver ci-joint...", "Je me permets de vous contacter...", "Dans l'attente de votre réponse...".

To refuse tactfully use the conditional: "Je crains de ne pas pouvoir...", "Il serait difficile de...". In meetings use "Je propose que nous...", "Pourriez-vous préciser?" Use "vous" unless a colleague invites "tu"; in many companies, "tu" is common among colleagues, so follow the culture of the workplace.
items: I allow myself to contact you
Je me permets de vous contacter
Je crains de ne pas pouvoir
sentences: I am afraid I cannot attend.

gq.q: Which closing is suitable for a business email?
Why does a polite refusal use the conditional?
gq.why: The conditional adds distance and politeness.

panel.q: After "Je propose que", which mood is required?
panel.why: Proposer que takes the subjunctive.

panel.q: What does "ci-joint" mean?
panel.why: Ci-joint is used for attachments.

panel.q: Why can using "tu" with a manager be risky?
o: It may be too familiar unless invited
panel.why: Workplace culture decides when tu is acceptable.

points.ask: How do I mention an attachment?

teach.model: Professional French is polite and indirect. Emails begin with Madame, Monsieur and end with Cordialement. Use ci-joint for attachments. Soften refusals with the conditional or je crains que.

stages.hook: How do you write "Please find attached the report" and refuse a request tactfully in a French office?
stages.mnemonic: Open politely, state the purpose, close with a courtesy.

stages.title: Literary analysis
explain: Literary analysis asks what a text does and how. Identify the narrator, point of view, structure, imagery and tone. Figures of speech include métaphore (identity), comparaison (like), personnification, hyperbole, antithèse and ellipse. In poetry, count syllables: the alexandre has twelve syllables.

Baudelaire's "Correspondances" (from "Les Fleurs du mal", 1857) suggests that senses answer each other. Camus's "L'Étranger" uses short sentences and a detached narrator to create distance. Léopold Sédar Senghor, Senegal's poet and first president, used rhythm and image to affirm African identity. Mariama Bâ's "Une si longue lettre" is a novel in the form of a letter.
sentences: The narrator keeps a cold distance.
The poem uses a strong metaphor.
Senghor was a poet and president.

gq.q: Which writer was both a poet and Senegal's first president?
Why does Camus use short, flat sentences in "L'Étranger"?
o: To create detachment and mirror the narrator's attitude
gq.why: Style reflects the narrator's emotional distance.

panel.q: How many syllables does a classical alexandrine have?
panel.why: The alexandrin has twelve syllables.

panel.q: What is the difference between metaphor and comparison?
o: A comparison uses a word like comme; a metaphor states identity
panel.why: Comparison is explicit with comme, metaphor implicit.

panel.q: Why is "Une si longue lettre" described as epistolary?
o: It is written as a letter
panel.why: Mariama Bâ's novel takes the form of a letter to a friend.

points.ask: How do I link style and meaning?

teach.model: To analyse a text, identify the narrator, point of view, structure, imagery and tone. Name figures such as métaphore and comparaison. Link technique to effect, for example short sentences creating distance in L'Étranger.

stages.hook: What is a metaphor doing in Baudelaire's line "La Nature est un temple"?
stages.mnemonic: Who speaks, how, and to what effect?

stages.title: Advanced listening comprehension
explain: Advanced listening needs prediction and inference. Listen first for the main idea, then for the speaker's attitude. French speech is full of enchaînement (linking consonants to the next vowel) and elision: "il y a" can sound like "ya", "je ne sais pas" like "chais pas".

Distinguish fact from opinion using markers: "selon", "d'après", "il paraît que". Note discourse markers: "bref" (in short), "en fait", "quoi" and "voilà". Take notes with abbreviations and write only key words.
sentences: According to him, the project is late.
It seems that prices will rise.

gq.q: What is a good first listening goal?
Why does "je ne sais pas" sometimes sound like "chais pas"?
o: Fast speech reduces and merges sounds
It is a mistake in writing

panel.q: What does "il paraît que" signal?
panel.why: It reports hearsay.

panel.q: Which word is a discourse marker meaning "in short"?
panel.why: Bref summarises.

panel.q: Why distinguish a speaker's fact from opinion?
o: It affects how you assess the message
panel.why: Understanding stance is part of comprehension.

points.ask: What do I listen for first?

teach.model: Listen first for the main idea and then for details and attitude. Notice reductions in fast speech and markers like selon, bref and il paraît que. Take brief notes with key words.

stages.hook: How can you follow a French radio interview when speakers use slang, hesitation and fast speech?
stages.mnemonic: Main idea first, then details, then attitude.

stages.title: Oral fluency and presentations
explain: Fluency comes from chunks and structure. Learn ready phrases such as "Ce qui est intéressant, c'est que...", "Pour commencer...", "Autrement dit...", "Pour résumer...". Use filler words with care: a few "euh" and "alors" are natural, many are distracting.

Prepare an opening, three points and a closing. Vary rhythm and use pauses. Pronunciation matters: keep liaison where it is required (les amis, un petit ami), avoid it in optional cases when informal, and remember that the unstressed e is often dropped in fast speech: "je ne sais pas" becomes "je n'sais pas".
items: ce qui est intéressant, c'est que
sentences: To begin with, I will define the topic.
To sum up, we have three options.

gq.q: What structure supports a short talk?
gq.why: A clear structure helps the audience.

gq.q: Why must liaison be avoided after "et"?
o: It is forbidden in this fixed case
It is optional only in song
gq.why: The word et never links to the next word.

panel.q: Which liaison is required?
panel.why: Article plus noun liaison is obligatory.

panel.q: What does the phrase "pour résumer" do?
panel.why: It works as a signpost.

panel.q: Why do fluent speakers use chunks?
panel.why: Retrieval of whole phrases speeds speech.

teach.model: Speak in chunks and structure your talk with an opening, points and closing. Use signposts like pour commencer and pour résumer. Keep required liaisons and vary rhythm.

stages.hook: How can you speak for three minutes in French without a script and still sound organised?
stages.mnemonic: Open, three points, close; breathe between them.

stages.title: Translation and interpretation
explain: Translation works on texts; interpretation works on speech in real time. Translators consider purpose, audience and register. They use strategies: transposition (changing word class), modulation (changing point of view) and équivalence (replacing an idiom). For example, "Attention, chien méchant" becomes "Beware of the dog", not a literal "Attention, nasty dog".

Interpreters work in consecutive mode (speaking after the speaker pauses) or simultaneous mode (almost at the same time). They take notes with symbols and rely on memory, concentration and general knowledge. Ethics: accuracy, confidentiality and impartiality.
sentences: The interpreter translates in real time.
The text keeps the same meaning.

o: Interpreting almost at the same time as the speaker
gq.why: The interpreter speaks while the speaker continues.

gq.q: Why is a literal translation of "Attention, chien méchant" risky?
o: A natural sign in English is "Beware of the dog"
gq.why: Translation should follow the convention of the target language.

panel.q: What is modulation?
o: Changing the point of view in expression
panel.why: Modulation expresses the same idea from another angle.

panel.q: Why are notes with symbols useful in consecutive interpreting?
o: They save time and support memory
panel.why: Symbols help recall ideas.

panel.q: Why is impartiality an ethical rule for interpreters?
o: They must not add personal opinion
panel.why: Faithful rendering respects all parties.

teach.model: Translation is written work and interpretation is spoken, in consecutive or simultaneous mode. Translators use transposition, modulation and équivalence to render meaning. Interpreters must be accurate, impartial and confidential.

stages.hook: A speaker says "On verra" and the interpreter has three seconds. How do you translate something that could mean "we'll see" or "maybe not"?
stages.mnemonic: Meaning first, form second, ethics always.

stages.title: Idiomatic and figurative language
explain: Idioms and figurative language carry cultural images. "Avoir un chat dans la gorge" means to have a frog in one's throat. "Tomber dans les pommes" means to faint. "Casser les pieds à quelqu'un" means to annoy someone. "Avoir le bras long" means to have influence.

Figurative language includes metonymy ("boire un verre" for drinking its contents), synecdoche, irony and litotes, which says less to mean more: "Ce n'est pas mauvais" means it is quite good. Proverbs also reflect shared values: "Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid" (little by little, the bird builds its nest).
items: to have a frog in one's throat
avoir un chat dans la gorge
sentences: Little by little, the bird builds its nest.
That is not bad at all!

gq.q: What does "tomber dans les pommes" mean?
gq.why: It is an idiom for fainting.

gq.q: What figure is "Ce n'est pas mauvais" meaning "it is good"?

panel.q: In "boire un verre" what is being named?
o: The container stands for its contents
panel.why: This is metonymy.

panel.q: Why can a literal translation of "casser les pieds" mislead?
panel.why: It means to annoy, not to break feet.

panel.q: Why do proverbs vary across cultures?
o: They reflect different environments and values
panel.why: Images come from local life.

teach.model: Idioms are fixed expressions with figurative meanings, like tomber dans les pommes for fainting. Figures include metonymy, irony and litotes. Learn expressions as whole units.

stages.hook: What does "avoir un chat dans la gorge" really mean, and why does a language use such images?
stages.mnemonic: Picture the image, then find the meaning.

stages.title: Extended independent writing
explain: Start with a plan: introduction (hook, context, problématique, annonce du plan), development (two or three parts, each with an argument, an example and a mini-conclusion), and a conclusion (answer and opening). Use topic sentences and transitions: "Tout d'abord", "En second lieu", "Enfin".

Style: vary sentence length, prefer precise verbs, and avoid repetition with synonyms and pronouns. Revise in rounds: structure, clarity, grammar, then spelling. Check participle agreement, subjunctive after "il faut que" and "bien que", and accents.
sentences: First, I present the main argument.
Finally, the conclusion answers the question.
A good plan guides the reader.

gq.q: Which part comes last in an essay plan?
gq.why: The conclusion answers the question and opens perspectives.

o: It is a rule of grammar

panel.q: Which sentence needs the subjunctive?
o: Bien que ce soit difficile, il continue.
Parce que c'est difficile, il continue.
panel.why: Bien que takes the subjunctive.

panel.q: What does "annonce du plan" do?
o: Tells the reader how the essay is organised
panel.why: It is the final part of the introduction.

panel.q: Why include an example in each part?
o: It makes the argument concrete and verifiable
panel.why: Examples support the claim.

points.ask: How do I improve a draft?

teach.model: Plan before writing: introduction with problématique, two or three developed parts, and a conclusion. Use topic sentences and transitions. Revise in rounds for structure, clarity, grammar and spelling.

stages.hook: How do you turn a rough idea into a clear, well-structured essay of about 500 words in French?
